aluminum has a great impact on its kinetics and effects. The Al3þ and Fe3þ ions, having the same valency and similar ionic radii,
engage in some of the same chemical and metabolic processes. Aluminum binds particularly strongly to phosphates, giving it the
potential to bind with deoxyribonucleic acid, adenosine triphosphate, and many other biomolecules.
In contrast to its abundance in the earth’s crust, natural waters contain little dissolved aluminum. Its average concentration in
lakes, rivers, ground water, coastal sea water, and open ocean water is 150, 400, 100, 1 to 7, and 1 mg L1, respectively. This is
a result of the low solubility of some aluminum salts and aluminum hydroxide deposition in sediments. Acidiﬁcation, e.g., by
acid rain and mine runoff, can solubilize aluminum and raise its concentrations in acidiﬁed lakes and rivers, producing toxicity
to aquatic organisms. Airborne aluminum from natural (soil-derived) and anthropogenic sources ranges from <1 ng/m3 in remote
sites to > 1 mg/m3 in industrialized locations. The World Health Organization (WHO) has a ‘practicable level’ in ﬁnished
(drinking) of 0.1 and  0.2 mg L1 for large and small water treatment facilities (WHO, 2004). The European Union (EU) “Indi-
cator Parameter” directive for aluminum in drinking water is 0.2 mg L1 (EU, 2020). The US Environmental Protection Agency has
a secondary, non-enforceable standard of 0.05–0.2 mg L1, based on esthetic (taste, sight, and smell) properties (US EPA, 2021
